```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(caTools)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Part 1: Reproduce the CART model from the Topic 3 demonstration

## Data preparation (as in the demo)

```{r data}
loandata <- read.csv("Loan_Delinquent_Dataset.csv")
for (v in c("isDelinquent", "term", "gender", "purpose", "home_ownership", "age", "FICO"))
  loandata[[v]] <- as.factor(loandata[[v]])
loandata <- loandata[, -1]                                   # drop ID
levels(loandata$purpose) <- c("Car", "House", "Medical", "Other", "Other",
                              "Personal", "Wedding")          # merge 'Other'/'other'

set.seed(1000)                                                # same seed as the demo
sample <- sample.split(loandata$isDelinquent, SplitRatio = 0.7)
train <- subset(loandata, sample == TRUE)
test  <- subset(loandata, sample == FALSE)
c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))
prop.table(table(train$isDelinquent))
```

The positive class throughout is **isDelinquent = 1**. A *false negative* is a
delinquent borrower the model lets through (predicts 0); a *false positive* is
a good borrower the model flags (predicts 1).

## The demo's CART model (Model 2)

```{r demo-model}
r.ctrl2 <- rpart.control(minsplit = 500, minbucket = 150, cp = 0, xval = 10)
model2 <- rpart(isDelinquent ~ ., data = train, method = "class", control = r.ctrl2)
model2
rpart.plot(model2, type = 4, extra = 104, main = "Demo CART (Model 2)")
```

## A deliberately over-grown tree

The demo's tree has few leaves because the controls (`minsplit = 500`) stop it
early. To see what pruning does, I also grow a maximal tree (every split
allowed, `cp = -1`) and prune it back in Part 2.

```{r full-tree}
set.seed(1000)
full <- rpart(isDelinquent ~ ., data = train, method = "class",
              control = rpart.control(minsplit = 2, minbucket = 1, cp = -1, xval = 10))
n_leaves <- function(m) sum(m$frame$var == "<leaf>")
n_leaves(full)
```

# Part 2: Prune using the cross-validated results

```{r printcp}
printcp(full)
```

```{r plotcp}
plotcp(full)
```

```{r choose-cp}
tb <- full$cptable
best_row <- which.min(tb[, "xerror"])
best_cp  <- tb[best_row, "CP"]
one_se   <- tb[best_row, "xerror"] + tb[best_row, "xstd"]
row_1se  <- min(which(tb[, "xerror"] <= one_se))
c(best_row = best_row, best_cp = best_cp, nsplit = tb[best_row, "nsplit"],
  min_xerror = tb[best_row, "xerror"], row_1se = row_1se)

pruned <- prune(full, cp = best_cp)
n_leaves(pruned)
rpart.plot(pruned, type = 4, extra = 104, main = "Pruned tree")
```

**Chosen cp = `r format(best_cp, scientific = FALSE, digits = 2)`.** The cross-validated error (`xerror`)
falls from 1.00 with no splits to `r round(tb[best_row, "xerror"], 3)` at
`r tb[best_row, "nsplit"]` splits, then stops improving and creeps back up
(`r round(tb[best_row + 1, "xerror"], 3)`) as more splits are allowed. I took
the row with the lowest `xerror`; the one-standard-error rule picks the same
row (row `r row_1se`), so there is no ambiguity. Pruning at this cp shrinks the
tree from `r n_leaves(full)` leaves to `r n_leaves(pruned)`, and any cp between
`r format(best_cp, scientific = FALSE, digits = 2)` and `r format(tb[best_row - 1, "CP"], digits = 2)` gives the same
tree. It uses only `FICO`, `gender`, `age` and `term`; `purpose` and
`home_ownership` never help.

# Part 3: Evaluate the pruned tree on the test data

```{r eval}
p_test  <- predict(pruned, test)[, "1"]          # P(delinquent)
actual  <- test$isDelinquent
make_tab <- function(p, cutoff) {
  pred <- factor(as.integer(p > cutoff), levels = 0:1)
  table(Actual = factor(actual, levels = 0:1), Predicted = pred)
}
metrics <- function(tab) {
  c(accuracy    = sum(diag(tab)) / sum(tab),
    sensitivity = tab["1", "1"] / sum(tab["1", ]),   # delinquents caught
    specificity = tab["0", "0"] / sum(tab["0", ]))   # good borrowers passed
}

tab50 <- make_tab(p_test, 0.5)
tab50
round(metrics(tab50), 4)
```

Sensitivity is the share of delinquent borrowers the tree flags; specificity is
the share of good borrowers it correctly lets through.

## ROC curve and AUC

```{r roc}
roc_at <- function(cutoff) {
  tab <- make_tab(p_test, cutoff)
  c(cutoff = cutoff, TPR = tab["1", "1"] / sum(tab["1", ]),
    FPR = tab["0", "1"] / sum(tab["0", ]))
}
cuts <- c(-Inf, sort(unique(p_test)), Inf)
roc <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(cuts, function(ct) {
  pred <- as.integer(p_test >= ct)             # flag everyone at or above the score
  c(cutoff = ct,
    TPR = sum(pred == 1 & actual == 1) / sum(actual == 1),
    FPR = sum(pred == 1 & actual == 0) / sum(actual == 0))
})))
roc <- roc[order(roc$FPR, roc$TPR), ]

# AUC = P(random delinquent scores higher than random good borrower), ties = 1/2
auc <- function(score, y) {
  r <- rank(score); n1 <- sum(y == 1); n0 <- sum(y == 0)
  (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
AUC <- auc(p_test, as.integer(as.character(actual)))
AUC
n_distinct_scores <- length(unique(p_test))

r50 <- roc_at(0.5); r16 <- roc_at(1/6)
pt <- data.frame(label = c("cutoff 0.50", "cutoff 1/6"),
                 TPR = c(r50[["TPR"]], r16[["TPR"]]),
                 FPR = c(r50[["FPR"]], r16[["FPR"]]))
ggplot(roc, aes(FPR, TPR)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_step(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1, direction = "vh") +
  geom_point(data = roc, colour = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = pt, aes(colour = label), size = 4) +
  labs(title = paste0("ROC curve, pruned tree (AUC = ", round(AUC, 3), ")"),
       x = "False positive rate (1 - specificity)",
       y = "True positive rate (sensitivity)", colour = "") +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Part 4: Business-rule memo

```{r rules}
rpart.rules(pruned, cover = TRUE)
```

> **Memo to loan officers** (rules from the pruned tree; share of past loans in
> brackets)
>
> 1. FICO 500 or below, 36-month term: **decline**. 90% went delinquent [52%].
> 2. FICO 500 or below, 60-month term: approve. None went delinquent [3%].
> 3. FICO above 500, female: approve. 23% delinquent [21%].
> 4. FICO above 500, male: a 36-month loan is risky if over 25 (79% delinquent)
>    but acceptable at 20-25 (30%). A 60-month loan is risky at 20-25 (85%) and
>    safe over 25 (none).
>
> **Caution:** the 60-month results are surprising, so check them. Gender and
> age drive rules 3 and 4, and lending law in many places forbids using them, so
> get legal review before use.

```{r memo-words, echo=FALSE}
memo <- "Memo to loan officers (rules from the pruned tree; share of past loans in brackets) 1. FICO 500 or below, 36-month term: decline. 90% went delinquent [52%]. 2. FICO 500 or below, 60-month term: approve. None went delinquent [3%]. 3. FICO above 500, female: approve. 23% delinquent [21%]. 4. FICO above 500, male: a 36-month loan is risky if over 25 (79% delinquent) but acceptable at 20-25 (30%). A 60-month loan is risky at 20-25 (85%) and safe over 25 (none). Caution: the 60-month results are surprising, so check them. Gender and age drive rules 3 and 4, and lending law in many places forbids using them, so get legal review before use."
word_count <- lengths(strsplit(memo, "\\s+"))
```

*Memo length: `r word_count` words (limit 150).*

# Written answers

## 1. What do the errors cost?

At the 0.5 cutoff the test set has **`r tab50["1", "0"]` false negatives** and
**`r tab50["0", "1"]` false positives**.

* **False negative (a delinquent borrower approved):** the lender loses the
  unrecovered principal and the cost of collections, and the loan adds to bad
  debt. The borrower is also harmed, because they take on debt they cannot repay.
* **False positive (a good borrower declined):** the borrower loses a loan they
  would have repaid, such as a house, car or medical need, and may turn to
  worse credit. The lender loses the interest and fee income that loan would
  have earned.

I would rather reduce **false negatives**. One missed delinquency usually costs
the lender a large part of the principal, while a wrongly declined loan costs
only the margin, so in money terms a false negative is the more expensive error.
The price is more false positives, so how far to push depends on the cost ratio
(next question). Declining good borrowers also has a fairness cost, so it
should not be ignored.

## 2. If a miss costs five times a wrong decline

Approving a borrower with delinquency probability $p$ has expected cost
$5p$ (a miss); declining has expected cost $1\times(1-p)$ (a wrong decline).
Decline whenever $5p > 1-p$, that is $p > 1/6 \approx 0.167$. In general the
threshold is $C_{FP}/(C_{FP}+C_{FN}) = 1/(1+5)$.

```{r threshold}
tab_c <- make_tab(p_test, 1/6)
tab_c
cmp <- rbind(`cutoff 0.50` = metrics(tab50), `cutoff 1/6` = metrics(tab_c))
cost <- function(tab) 5 * tab["1", "0"] + 1 * tab["0", "1"]
cmp <- cbind(round(cmp, 4), FN = c(tab50["1", "0"], tab_c["1", "0"]),
             FP = c(tab50["0", "1"], tab_c["0", "1"]),
             total_cost = c(cost(tab50), cost(tab_c)))
cmp
```

At the 1/6 cutoff sensitivity moves from
`r round(metrics(tab50)["sensitivity"], 3)` to
`r round(metrics(tab_c)["sensitivity"], 3)` and specificity from
`r round(metrics(tab50)["specificity"], 3)` to
`r round(metrics(tab_c)["specificity"], 3)`. The total cost (in units of one
wrongly declined loan) goes from `r cost(tab50)` to `r cost(tab_c)`, a change
of `r round(100 * (cost(tab_c) - cost(tab50)) / cost(tab50), 1)`%. The tree has
only `r n_distinct_scores` distinct scores, so moving the cutoff from 0.5 to
1/6 changes which leaves are flagged, and changes accuracy
(`r round(metrics(tab50)["accuracy"], 3)` to
`r round(metrics(tab_c)["accuracy"], 3)`), but it cannot change anything in
between.

## 3. What does the ROC curve show?

A confusion matrix is one point: it fixes a single cutoff. The ROC curve shows
sensitivity against the false-positive rate at **every** cutoff, so it shows
the whole trade-off and lets you choose a cutoff after the costs are known. It
also does not depend on class balance.

**AUC = `r round(AUC, 3)`.** As a probability: if I pick one delinquent and one
non-delinquent borrower at random from the test set, there is a
`r round(100 * AUC, 1)`% chance the tree gives the delinquent borrower the
higher risk score (ties count half). 0.5 is a coin flip and 1 is perfect.

A tree gives so few points because every borrower who lands in the same leaf
gets the same score (the leaf's class proportion). This tree has
`r n_leaves(pruned)` leaves but only `r n_distinct_scores` distinct scores, so
the ROC curve has only `r n_distinct_scores + 1` corners instead of a smooth
curve. Many ties also mean the tree cannot rank borrowers inside a leaf.

## 4. Full tree vs pruned tree

```{r gap}
acc <- function(m, dat) mean(predict(m, dat, type = "class") == dat$isDelinquent)
gap <- data.frame(
  Tree = c("Full (maximal)", "Pruned"),
  Leaves = c(n_leaves(full), n_leaves(pruned)),
  Train_accuracy = round(c(acc(full, train), acc(pruned, train)), 4),
  Test_accuracy = round(c(acc(full, test), acc(pruned, test)), 4))
gap$Gap_train_minus_test <- gap$Train_accuracy - gap$Test_accuracy
gap
```

The full tree has `r n_leaves(full)` leaves and scores
`r round(100 * acc(full, train), 2)`% on training data against
`r round(100 * acc(full, test), 2)`% on test data, a gap of
`r round(100 * (acc(full, train) - acc(full, test)), 2)` points. The pruned tree
has `r n_leaves(pruned)` leaves and scores
`r round(100 * acc(pruned, train), 2)`% against
`r round(100 * acc(pruned, test), 2)`%, a gap of
`r round(100 * (acc(pruned, train) - acc(pruned, test)), 2)` points. So here
pruning removes `r n_leaves(full) - n_leaves(pruned)` leaves without losing
accuracy. The gap is small in both cases because the data has only six
categorical predictors with few distinct combinations, so there is little
noise for a tree to memorise. The over-grown tree is still not better, only
bigger and harder to explain.

**What cp controls:** `cp` is the complexity penalty. A split is kept only if
it lowers the tree's error by at least `cp` times the root error, so a larger
cp gives a smaller tree, and `cp = 0` allows any split. **What `xerror` says:**
it is the 10-fold cross-validated error, relative to the root (one-leaf)
tree, so `r round(tb[best_row, "xerror"], 3)` means the tree makes
`r round(100 * tb[best_row, "xerror"], 1)`% as many mistakes as always guessing
the majority class. `xstd` is its standard error. The `xerror` falls until
about `r tb[best_row, "nsplit"]` splits and then flattens and rises, which is
the sign that further splits only fit noise, and I prune where it is lowest.

## 5. Instability: would the rules change on different data?

I refit the whole procedure (grow the maximal tree, choose cp by cross-validated
error, prune) on 100 bootstrap resamples of the training data, and on 100
random samples of only 1,000 loans.

```{r stability, cache=TRUE}
refit <- function(dat) {
  m <- rpart(isDelinquent ~ ., data = dat, method = "class",
             control = rpart.control(minsplit = 2, minbucket = 1, cp = -1, xval = 10))
  t <- m$cptable
  p <- prune(m, cp = t[which.min(t[, "xerror"]), "CP"])
  vars <- sort(unique(as.character(p$frame$var[p$frame$var != "<leaf>"])))
  list(root = as.character(p$frame$var[1]),
       vars = paste(vars, collapse = "+"),
       leaves = sum(p$frame$var == "<leaf>"),
       test_acc = mean(predict(p, test, type = "class") == test$isDelinquent))
}
summarise_runs <- function(res) {
  data.frame(
    root_FICO_pct = 100 * mean(sapply(res, `[[`, "root") == "FICO"),
    same_4_vars_pct = 100 * mean(sapply(res, `[[`, "vars") == "age+FICO+gender+term"),
    core_always_pct = 100 * mean(grepl("age", sapply(res, `[[`, "vars")) &
                                 grepl("FICO", sapply(res, `[[`, "vars")) &
                                 grepl("gender", sapply(res, `[[`, "vars")) &
                                 grepl("term", sapply(res, `[[`, "vars"))),
    distinct_variable_sets = length(unique(sapply(res, `[[`, "vars"))),
    exactly_7_leaves_pct = 100 * mean(sapply(res, `[[`, "leaves") == 7),
    leaves_min = min(sapply(res, `[[`, "leaves")),
    leaves_max = max(sapply(res, `[[`, "leaves")),
    test_acc_min = round(min(sapply(res, `[[`, "test_acc")), 3),
    test_acc_max = round(max(sapply(res, `[[`, "test_acc")), 3))
}
set.seed(2026)
boot <- lapply(1:100, function(i) refit(train[sample(nrow(train), replace = TRUE), ]))
small <- lapply(1:100, function(i) refit(train[sample(nrow(train), 1000), ]))
stab <- rbind(`Bootstrap (n = 8084)` = summarise_runs(boot),
              `Small samples (n = 1000)` = summarise_runs(small))
stab
table(Variables_used = sapply(small, `[[`, "vars"))
```

The top of the tree is stable. `FICO` is the root split in
`r stab[1, "root_FICO_pct"]`% of bootstrap runs and `r stab[2, "root_FICO_pct"]`%
of small-sample runs, and `FICO`, `gender`, `age` and `term` were all used in
`r stab[1, "core_always_pct"]`% and `r stab[2, "core_always_pct"]`% of runs.

The detail is not stable. Only `r stab[1, "same_4_vars_pct"]`% of bootstrap runs
and `r stab[2, "same_4_vars_pct"]`% of small-sample runs use exactly those four
variables; in the others, `purpose` and/or `home_ownership` also enter the tree
(`r stab[2, "distinct_variable_sets"]` different variable sets in the small
samples). The pruned tree has exactly 7 leaves, like mine, in only
`r stab[1, "exactly_7_leaves_pct"]`% of bootstrap runs and
`r stab[2, "exactly_7_leaves_pct"]`% of small-sample runs, and its size ranges
from `r stab[1, "leaves_min"]` to `r stab[1, "leaves_max"]` leaves (bootstrap)
and `r stab[2, "leaves_min"]` to `r stab[2, "leaves_max"]` (small samples), so
the deeper rules are different in different samples. Test accuracy barely
moves (`r stab[1, "test_acc_min"]` to `r stab[1, "test_acc_max"]` for the
bootstrap; `r stab[2, "test_acc_min"]` to `r stab[2, "test_acc_max"]` for small
samples), so the *predictions* are stable even where the *rules* are not. This
is the usual instability of trees: small changes in the data change which weak
splits win, even when overall performance does not change.

This matters before a lender adopts the memo because the memo is a list of
rules, and a rule that depends on the particular sample may not hold on next
year's loans. I would adopt the top-level rules (`FICO`, then `term`) with
more confidence than the deeper ones, check the 60-month results on a fresh
sample from a later period before relying on them, and report the rules with
their uncertainty. If stability matters more than readability, an ensemble such
as a random forest would be steadier but is harder to hand to a loan officer.
Gender and age also need legal review whatever the data shows.
